question_en: A company issued a 2-year bond and chose not to make cash interest payments prior to maturity. Instead, the company elected to add additional debt to the principal amount each period. The company payed off the full principal at maturity. This type of bond is best described as a:
explanation_en: A callable bond contains a call provision that gives the issuer (ie, borrower) the option to buy back the bond from the bondholder (ie, investor) at a predetermined price prior to maturity. The issuer may exercise the call option (ie, call the bond) when interest rates fall and then refinance the bond at a lower interest rate. This exposes the investor to reinvestment risk since the proceeds must be reinvested at lower rates. Therefore, the call feature benefits the issuer at the investor's expense. However, due to the reinvestment risk, investors pay less for callable bonds than for otherwise similar option-free bonds. Likewise, callable bonds earn higher yields. To mitigate their risk, these bonds sometimes contain a call protection period (ie, lockout period) that prohibits exercising the call option until a specified date. (Choices A and C) The issuer has the option to redeem (ie, buy back) the bond at the predetermined call price, which is at least equal to the par value.

explanation_en: Types of call provisions American style Continuously callable: the issuer has the right to call at any time beginning on the call date until maturity European style Only one call date, and the issuer can call bonds only on that date Bermuda style Can be called on one of multiple call dates, but only on those dates A callable bond gives the issuer the right to buy the bond from the bondholders prior to maturity, which exposes bondholders to the risk of then reinvesting at lower yields. Investors will require incrementally higher yields to compensate for any increased risk of exercise; therefore, the more flexibility the issuer embeds with the call option, the higher the cost (ie, the bond yield) will be to the issuer. An American-style call provision is often referred to as continuously callable since the issuer has the right to call bonds at any time beginning on the call date until final maturity. Of the three types of calls, an American-style call gives the issuer the most flexibility and exposes the investor to the most risk. Therefore, American-style bonds are the most expensive to issue since investors will require the highest yield to compensate for their risk. (Choice A) A Bermuda-style call provision has multiple call dates, but bonds can be called only on a specific call date, which often matches coupon payment dates. (Choice C) A European-style call provision exposes the investor to the least amount of call risk since there is only one call date and the issuer can call the bonds only on that date.

explanation_en: Bond indentures Obligations of issuers Contracts Rights of bondholders Due dates of interest and principal Cash flows Amounts due or method of determination Affirmative: Actions the issuer must take Covenants Negative: Actions the issuer is prohibited from taking Seniority of bond issue Credit protections Assets pledged as collateral or credit enhancements Bondholder options: Put or conversion provisions Contingency provisions Issuer options: Call provisions Indentures (eg, bond indentures, trust deeds) are contracts that specify the terms and conditions regarding repayment of debt securities. A bond indenture identifies: the rights of bondholders, the obligations of the issuer, and a trustee to monitor and enforce the issuer's compliance with the contract. Bond indentures also specify the amount and timing of the interest and principal repayments along with the source(s) of funds to meet those obligations. Credit ratings reflect a rating agency's assessment of the bond issuer's ability to make the payments in accordance with the terms stated in the indenture. Appraising a bond's creditworthiness involves assessing any protective provisions included in the indenture, but the credit rating itself is not an element of the indenture. (Choice A) Most indentures include covenants that protect bondholders by placing restrictions (eg, limits on dividends) and/or requirements (eg, maintain minimum net worth) on the issuer. (Choice C) Many indentures include contingency provisions granting the issuer and/or the bondholders options to take some action (eg, allowing the issuer to retire bonds prior to maturity).

question_en: A bond indenture is least likely to include:
explanation_en: A convertible bond is a hybrid security that has both debt and equity characteristics. It is issued as a straight bond, so it has a par value (ie, face value) and a maturity date. However, a convertible bond gives the owner the option to convert it into a specific number of shares of the issuer's common stock. The conversion feature can benefit the owner, since the company's stock may generate a greater return than the bond. This benefit permits the issuer to pay a lower coupon rate than for a nonconvertible bond. The bond's indenture (contract) may provide the number of shares (conversion ratio) and the per-share price (conversion price) of the common stock that the bond can be converted into. If the bond does not specify a conversion ratio, it can be calculated by dividing the bond's par value by the conversion price. Since this bond's conversion price is £40, the conversion ratio equals 25 (£1,000 ÷ £40). (Choice A) 23.75 results from incorrectly dividing the bond's current price (£950)—rather than its par value—by the conversion price. (Choice C) 33.33 results from dividing the bond's par value by the stock's current price (£30) instead of its conversion price (£40).

question_en: A bond issued by New York City, denominated in USD, and sold only in Canada and Mexico is most likely a:
explanation_en: A bond with a deferred coupon pays no coupon interest early in its life and compensates investors with a higher coupon rate in later years. The most common application of deferred coupon bonds is allowing better cash flow management in project financing, as in this scenario. Due to the lack of coupon payments early in their life, deferred coupon bonds are most often issued at a significant discount to par. A zero-coupon bond can be thought of as an extreme example of a deferred coupon bond since all principal and interest is deferred until final maturity. (Choice A) A step-up coupon bond increases the coupon at a predetermined rate at specified intervals. Step-up bonds are often callable by the issuer just before a scheduled increase in the coupon rate. This call flexibility gives the issuer the opportunity to refinance the loan at a lower rate if interest rates have not increased. (Choice C) A payment-in-kind (PIK) bond allows the issuer to pay coupon interest in cash or in additional bonds. PIK bonds are among the most expensive types of debt a company can issue and are most commonly issued by low-rated or distressed companies with a high debt burden. PIK bonds are much more likely to be used to fund a leveraged buyout (LBO) than to be used in project financing by an investment-grade issuer.

question_en: An investment-grade corporate bond issuer needs capital to fund a project that will not produce cash flow for several years. If the issuer wishes to align coupon payments with the project cash flows, which of the following bond coupon structures best fits this need?
explanation_en: Bonds with contingency provisions combine the cash flows of a debt contract with an option referred to as an embedded option. Three common examples are: callable bonds, which issuers can retire prior to maturity, putable bonds, which holders can force issuers to repurchase prior to maturity, and convertible bonds, which holders can exchange for issuers' common stock. Owning an option provides an advantage, so the effective price of such bonds reflects whichever counterparty is implicitly "paying" for the embedded option. Since issuers must pay for the right to retire bonds early, the issuer compensates investors by selling the bonds at a lower effective price and at a higher yield than equivalent noncallable (eg, putable, convertible) bonds. (Choices A and C) In putable and convertible bonds, investors own the option. Investors must pay the issuer a higher effective price for those rights, which is reflected in a lower yield compared with bonds not containing such options.

question_en: All else being equal, for an issuer selling 10-year bonds, which of the following most likely requires the highest yield at issuance? A bond that is:
explanation_en: A step-up coupon bond has a structure where the coupon increases by a predetermined amount on specific dates. These step-up dates usually correspond with call dates, allowing the issuer to call the bonds before the coupon increases. A step-up coupon structure offers investors some protection against rising interest rates but also exposes them to call risk. (Choice B) Coupons on floating-rate bonds reset periodically, but the amount of change is not preset. Floating-rate coupons are specifically tied to an underlying reference rate (eg, LIBOR), with the coupon fixed at that variable rate plus a predetermined spread. (Choice C) Bermuda style refers to a type of call structure in which the issuer has the right to call the bonds on predetermined dates (eg, quarterly), often in conjunction with coupon payment dates. However, the coupon is not scheduled to increase on each call date.

question_en: A one-year bond is issued with the following characteristics: This coupon structure is best described as:
explanation_en: Receipt of coupon interest and principal exposes investors to two potential types of tax. Interest is normally treated as ordinary income and is subject to tax at the same rate as wages. However, interest received on bonds issued by state and local governments is generally exempt from income tax. Tax-exempt bonds tend to be purchased by investors in jurisdictions with high personal income tax rates. The other type of tax is capital gains tax, which taxes an investor's gain (ie, profit) from an investment. This tax applies to all bonds, regardless of whether the bondholder pays taxes on interest received. A capital gain occurs when the face value that the investor receives at maturity is greater than the amount the investor paid for the bond. For the exam, remember that the tax-exempt designation does not apply to all taxes. The exemption usually applies to income taxation of coupon interest. Taxes on capital gains apply to all bonds (Choices A and C).

explanation_en: The interest and/or principal payments for index-linked bonds can vary based on changes to a specific index, such as a broad equity index or an index of commodities prices. Most index-linked bonds are designed to maintain purchasing power that erodes from inflation. When inflation increases, interest rates often rise too. Bonds that adjust their coupon interest rate and/or face value for inflation can help mitigate that risk. Inflation-linked bonds, a common category of index-linked bonds, are usually issued by sovereign governments. Adjustments to their coupon and/or principal payments are based on broad inflation indices such as the Consumer Price Index in the United States or the Retail Price Index in the UK. (Choice A) Callable bonds can be redeemed by the issuer before maturity (eg, refinancing when interest rates decline). Callability benefits the issuer (borrower), not the investors (lenders), since the issuer will call the bond when interest rates are declining. (Choice C) Payment-in-kind (PIK) bonds pay interest in the form of additional bonds rather than cash coupon payments. This feature can help issuers conserve cash by issuing more debt, but it exposes the investors to higher default risk since the issuer must repay more debt. PIK bonds' value does not increase when interest rates increase since the bonds do not adjust interest and/or principal in response to higher interest rates.

A domestic bond is issued by a company that is incorporated within the country of issuance, denominated in that country's currency, and sold to investors within that country. This classification applies even if the issuer is a subsidiary of a foreign company. An example is a US subsidiary of Toyota (a Japanese company) issuing USD bonds in the United States. explanation_en: A credit-linked bond has coupon payments that change as the bond's or issuer's credit rating changes. In this question, the coupon rate increases by 30 bps every time the issuer credit rating deteriorates. Investors may be concerned about an issuer's (borrower's) future creditworthiness, so credit-linked coupons compensate for this risk. question_en: A bond indenture specifies that the coupon rate will increase by 30 basis points (bps) every time the issuer receives a downgrade. This bond is most likely a:
explanation_en: A step-up coupon bond may have either fixed or a floating coupon. The main characteristic of a step-up coupon bond is that the coupon rate increases by a predetermined rate at specified intervals. Step-up bonds are often callable by the issuer just before a scheduled increase in the coupon rate. (Choice A) An inflation-linked bond offers investors protection against inflation, but changes in the coupon rate are tied to changes in inflation rather than being regularly scheduled. explanation_en: A sinking fund arrangement details a schedule for gradually retiring a bond's principal over time. The example above shows a plan to reduce principal by 10% annually after Year 5 and fully retire the bond in Year 15. For the issuer (ie, borrower), a sinking fund provides a well-timed, disciplined approach to retiring debt. The typical fixed-rate bond has relatively small periodic interest obligations and a large terminal principal (ie, face value) obligation. An issuer who implements a sinking fund provision can ease the payment schedule by reducing the principal early on, thus lowering the size of the terminal obligation (Choice C). For the bondholder (ie, investor), this provision can be both beneficial and detrimental. A detailed plan for repaying principal reduces the investor's exposure to credit risk (Choice B). However, early principal repayment increases reinvestment risk since the proceeds must be reinvested at a different—and perhaps lower—interest rate.

option_c: a larger balloon payment at maturity.
explanation_en: A putable bond contains a provision (ie, put provision) that gives the bondholder (ie, investor) the option to sell back the bond to the issuer at a predetermined price prior to maturity. A bondholder may choose to exercise the put option (ie, put the bond back to the issuer) when interest rates rise since rising rates lower the bond's value (Choice A). This benefit may allow the bondholder to sell the bond at a predetermined price that is higher than the market price and subsequently reinvest the proceeds at a higher interest rate. Since this benefit is bestowed on the bondholder, a putable bond is priced higher than an otherwise similar option-free bond and offers lower yields (Choice C). In effect, the bondholder pays a higher price to the issuer for the option to retire the bond early.

explanation_en: Make-whole call provision Lump-sum payment is equal to the present value of all forgone coupon and principal payments. Lump-sum payment is discounted at the YTM of a predetermined comparable government bond plus a spread. A call provision gives the issuer the option to buy back a bond before maturity. A make-whole call provision requires the issuer to make a lump- sum payment to bondholders that includes compensation for forgone coupon and principal payments and, thus, to make the bondholders whole if the bond is called. The lump-sum payment is calculated as the present value of all remaining future coupon and principal payments, discounted at a rate equal to the YTM of a predetermined comparable government bond plus a spread. The make-whole call can typically be exercised at any time and the payment can never be less than par. A call provision is seldom used since the cost to the issuer is usually substantial, but the provision is included in the bond indenture to "sweeten" the deal and lower the issuer's borrowing cost. In this scenario, the bond was issued with a 40-basis-point call spread (ie, 0.40%), which is added to the current 3.00% YTM of the referenced government bond. Therefore, the present value of the lump sum payment would be discounted at a rate of 3.40%. (Choice A) 2.90% results from inappropriately using the difference in yields (ie, yield spread) between the corporate bond and the government bond (2.50%) and adding the make-whole call spread of 40 basis points. (Choice C) 5.40% results from inappropriately using the corporate coupon rate of 5.00% and adding the make-whole call spread of 40 basis points.

question_en: A company issues a callable 10-year corporate bond with the following characteristics: The bond has a make-whole provision with a 40-basis-point call spread. If this bond is called, the unpaid coupons and principal will be discounted at a rate closest to:
explanation_en: Eurobond market Market Part of international bond market outside national markets' jurisdiction Currency Major currency (usually not issuer's domestic currency) denomination Issuance currency's benchmark rate + Yield spread reflecting Valuation issuer's credit risk and issue's liquidity risk The market value of a bond is the PV of the coupon and principal amounts discounted by the appropriate market interest rate for the bond's currency denomination. An interest rate in the same currency must be used since it represents the opportunity cost of debt capital in that currency. The specific rate used to value the bond is based on the currency's benchmark (eg, government bond, interest rate swap) rate, adjusted for any risk factors (eg, credit, liquidity) that are appropriate for the bond. A bond's market yield is the market discount rate used for valuing the bond's cash flows. Therefore, the market yield on US dollar-denominated emerging market sovereign debt, as in this case, is primarily determined by US dollar interest rates regardless of where the bonds are issued. (Choice A) Euro interest rates are used to value euro-denominated securities but have no direct effect on the value of bonds denominated in other currencies. The Eurobond market is a segment of the global fixed-income securities markets that consists of debt issued outside the jurisdiction of any single country. (Choice C) An emerging market's domestic interest rates are the primary determinant of the country's sovereign debt yield if the bond is denominated in that country's currency, regardless of where the debt is issued. However, in this scenario, the bonds are US dollar-denominated.

explanation_en: The coupon rate of a floating rate note (FRN) is reset regularly and often, typically every three months, based on market rates. Therefore, increased volatility in interest rates between coupon dates will not have much impact on the price of an FRN. If the issuer's credit quality has not changed, the price of the bond is equal to par value at each reset. Callable and putable bonds have embedded call and put options. Whether those options are exercised depends on interest rates. A rise in interest rate volatility increases the range of possible interest rates. With more possible outcomes, there is a higher probability that a bond's option will be exercised, which makes the option worth more. Interest rate volatility affects the prices of both callable and putable bonds. The price of a putable bond is the price of an otherwise identical option-free bond plus the value of the put option. As the put option increases in value, the price of the bond rises. The opposite applies for callable bonds: An increase in the value of the call option reduces the price of the bond (Choices A and B).

explanation_en: Types of call provisions American style Continuously callable: the issuer has the right to call at any time beginning on the call date until maturity European style Only one call date, and the issuer can call bonds only on that date Bermuda style Can be called on one of multiple call dates, but only on those dates A call provision allows the bond issuer to redeem a bond prior to its final maturity. This allowance exposes bondholders to reinvestment risk, as the call provision is unlikely to be exercised unless yields are lower than when the bond was issued. To compensate for the call risk, investors require higher yields for callable bonds than for noncallable bonds. Most callable bonds have an initial call protection period during which the bonds cannot be called. Once the call protection period has passed, the bond is callable within the constraints of the embedded call provision. Specific call dates usually coincide with coupon payment dates. In this scenario, the bond is callable on multiple specific dates and is, therefore, a Bermuda-style call rather than an American- or European- style call (Choices B and C). Bermuda-style calls often require a premium to par on the earliest call dates, which serves as a "sweetener" for the bondholder since it discourages the issuer from exercising the call provision early in the life of the bond.
